title: Protection of Hot News under the Broadcasting Laws in India
summary: This article asks whether broadcasters in India can stop rivals from free-riding on “hot news”: time-sensitive information whose commercial value lies in being first, such as updates from a live telecast. It traces the American doctrine of hot news misappropriation, its acceptance by Indian courts, and the 2013 shift that allowed others to disseminate such news freely. Examining copyright, contract and tort law alongside the Constitution of India, the authors conclude that Indian law already contains enough provisions to protect hot news.
citation: Raman Mittal and Satyarth Kuhad, “Protection of Hot News under the Broadcasting Laws in India”, 29(5) Journal of Intellectual Property Rights 375–388 (2024), https://doi.org/10.56042/jipr.v29i5.4017

title: Freedom and Copyright Law: Examining from the Perspective of Human Rights
summary: The article reads copyright law through three aspects of freedom: “freedom from” bondage, “freedom for” creative expression, and “freedom about”, the right of everyone to take part in the cultural life of the community. Mapping these onto the three generations of human rights and Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, it argues that copyright protects the flowering of creativity, while fair dealing, compulsory licences and the limited term of protection secure the duty to share. It concludes that ownership and sharing must go together, and that copyright rests on a balance between the author's rights and the wider public interest.
citation: Raman Mittal, Freedom and Copyright Law: Examining from the Perspective of Human Rights, VI SML. L. REV. 191 (2023), https://doi.org/10.70556/hpnlu-slr-v6-I1-2023-07
